abstract:
Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough.

Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory.

Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle’s progress).

Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.

sections.body: The paper asks whether published methods for ultrasound view matching, combined into one guide, are good enough. It introduces USB Gym, a closed-loop testbed on patient CT where published methods can replace guide components and be scored against a privileged pose oracle on identical episodes. From a 16.0 mm start on six held-out patients, the pose oracle ends at 1.5 mm, while the CT-mask servo ends at 11.6 to 11.8 mm. With SonoSPADE as the texture stage, the learned-mask servo ends at 13.1 mm. All closed-loop results come from simulation with rigid tissue, and no clinical usability is claimed.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Published ultrasound guidance parts had no shared closed loop for comparison, so the paper provides one.

sections.body: The related work covers ultrasound simulators, learned texture stages, learned probe navigation, visual servoing and runnable testbeds. Learned navigation methods are each trained and evaluated in their own environment. One later agent reached 75.8% success on a phantom and 74.0% on a cadaver. Table 1 compares runnable ultrasound navigation environments. Only USB Gym swaps published methods in six components, including the mask source and reward, and evaluates them on identical episodes against privileged references. Elsewhere in Table 1, published methods occupy at most the policy and the image source.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Existing ultrasound simulators, learned navigation methods and runnable testbeds each cover only part of the guide.

sections.body: USB Gym keeps every component of a closed ultrasound loop fixed except the one a user replaces, so a change in final error can be traced to that component. The task is a Gymnasium environment in which the probe moves from a perturbed start to a target view. Starts lie within ±20 mm lateral and elevational, ±10 mm axial, ±18° of tilt and ±4° of roll. Each step commands at most 3 mm along and 0.05 rad about each axis, and episodes are truncated at 12 steps. The contact plane through the target window face is privileged structure, tangent to the skin at only 15 of the 60 evaluation windows. The task is local re-acquisition near a known window; finding a window from afar is out of scope.
sections.heading: USB Gym: testbed design
sections.headline: Each USB Gym step renders a CT label slice, and the guide's mask source, controller and reward can each be replaced.

sections.body: A controller receives the observation and returns a normalized twist, and each step's reward is the gain in the match score minus the action cost. In the CT-free configuration, organ masks come from a learned segmenter, and no pose or CT mask reaches the controller or the reward. The segmenters and servo base were still fit with CT labels and true poses of training patients. Under the plug protocol, one slot is swapped at a time and the rest of the loop is held at its reference condition. Reinforcement learners get 57,600 environment steps, and imitation learners get 40,000 samples. Learned methods run seeds 0 to 2, and some run seed 0 only. Compute was measured on one Apple M5 Pro laptop, where training one reference policy took a median 0.79 h with CT masks.
sections.heading: Interface, plug protocol and compute
sections.headline: Each plugged method runs untuned on the same 60 held-out episodes, at 12 steps, with fixed settings and matched training budgets.

sections.body: The servo base adapts the Mebarki et al. servo, fitting by least squares on 500 training frame pairs a map from per-organ mask moments to the analytic twist. A residual, bounded at half the twist bound, is trained by REINFORCE with an imitation anchor, and only training uses the true pose. Each arm runs 60 crossed episodes per seed: six held-out patients by two organs by five windows. The primary metric is final translation error in mm. The oracle ladder orders rungs by how much simulator state each sees, from the pose oracle down to a static probe. Primary results use a pre-specified patient-cluster bootstrap rule. Exploratory analyses use a paired t rule with Holm adjustment, and the smallest exact sign-flip p is 2/64 at n = 6.
sections.heading: Reference pipeline and evaluation design
sections.headline: The reference controller adds a bounded learned residual to a servo base, scored by final translation error over 60 crossed episodes.

sections.body: From a static start of 16.03 mm, the pose oracle reaches 1.53 mm. The CT-mask servo base ends at 11.65 mm, and its final policies end at 11.64 to 11.81 mm. The oracle-to-CT-mask gap is +10.11 to +10.28 mm in every texture setting, with 6/6 patients sharing the sign. Imitation and REINFORCE each change the final translation error by less than 0.5 mm. With learned masks, SonoSPADE's final error is 13.11 mm. Its difference from the other stages is -3.38 to -3.78 mm, with 5/6 patients sharing the sign. These are pre-specified results, and every contrast is conditional on the trained artifacts.
sections.heading: Results: the reference pipeline
sections.headline: The CT-mask servo stays far from the pose oracle, and SonoSPADE gives the lowest learned-mask final error.

sections.body: Each slot's published methods were compared with its reference under one protocol. The benchmark baseline changes only the reward slot, to the SSIM appearance term, a choice that rests on a small difference of -0.047 mm under privileged CT masks. On 20 new CTs, the SonoSPADE combination ends at 13.70 mm [12.68, 14.73], which is 0.26 mm lower than the authors' original pipeline and 12.24 mm above the pose oracle. The combination was fixed before its runs using the six held-out patients. No published component, alone or combined, closes the gap to the pose oracle. Every result here is exploratory, and the post hoc minimum detectable differences run from 0.085 to 2.14 mm.
sections.heading: Results: published methods in the guide’s three slots
sections.headline: Of 19 contrasts in the guide's three slots, 4 differ and 15 do not, under exploratory rules.

sections.body: On 20 new CTs, the physics servo's gap from CT masks to learned masks is +2.57 [+1.66, +3.47], with 19/20 patients sharing the sign, against +4.92 with 5/6 on the six patients. SonoSPADE minus physics with the learned-mask servo base is -2.04 [-2.75, -1.33], with 17/20. On 30 external AMOS CTs, learned minus CT masks for physics is +4.01 [+3.40, +4.62], with 29/30. A PPO learner ends at 2.40 to 2.58 mm in 3 of 3 seeds on a privileged easy variant, so the training loop can learn a correction. REINFORCE removes 0.32 to 0.38 of a planted lateral deficit, positive in 0 of 6 patients, so that control is inconclusive.
sections.heading: Controls, sensitivity analyses and replication
sections.headline: Replication on 20 new CTs and 30 external CTs keeps the main contrast's direction, while the planted-deficit control is inconclusive.

sections.body: The answer to the research question is no: plugged one slot at a time, published components did not close the gap to the pose oracle. Most of the error, +10.1 to +10.3 mm, lies between the pose oracle and the CT-mask servo, and its cause is not attributed. The CT-to-learned-mask gap is the second limit, at +4.80 to +5.26 mm for three of four stages on the nearly isoechoic default render. Without privileged input, no level of the ladder succeeded at 5 mm and 5° in over 5.6% of episodes. The paper advises reporting a new method from at least three training seeds with its interval, not as a ranking, because n=6 is small. Stated limits include rigid tissue, no hardware test and the authorship overlap with SonoSPADE.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Published components plugged one slot at a time did not close the gap to the pose oracle, so the task remains under-explored.

sections.body: Plugged one slot at a time, untuned and at the reference training budget, existing published components did not close the gap to the pose oracle in this simulator. The benchmark baseline, a slot combination with an SSIM reward, reached 13.70 mm on the standard engine, against a pose oracle at 1.47 mm. This result is exploratory and conditional on this renderer. Its 0.26 mm lead over the reference pipeline lies within ±1 mm and is not attributed to SSIM. Of 19 contrasts in the guide's slots, 4 differed detectably and 15 did not. Of those 15, 2 lay within ±1 mm, and 13 were inconclusive at n=6. No policy was run on hardware, so a phantom or robot test is the next step.
sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.headline: The testbed accepts new components in each slot, and no policy was run on hardware.

sections.body: The code, tests and documentation are public under the Apache License 2.0. Each Zenodo release rebuilds every table and figure data file from the archived results. A second Zenodo record holds the result files behind every table. CT anatomy comes from the TotalSegmentator dataset under CC BY 4.0, and the 30 external CTs come from AMOS 2022. Real kidney frames come from KidneyUS under CC BY-NC-SA, granted only after registration and manual approval, and segmenter weights trained on KidneyUS are not released. Real liver frames come from the Annotated Ultrasound Liver dataset under CC BY 4.0. Third-party methods keep their own licenses.
sections.heading: Data and software availability
sections.headline: Code, result files and rebuild scripts are public, while some source datasets have restricted access.

sections.body: The results use only public, de-identified datasets. No new human or animal data were collected, and no experiment involved human participants. Ethical approval was therefore not sought. The real frames serve only as real targets, and all closed-loop results come from simulation. The statement covers the public CT, frame and label data that the study read, and not any new collection.
sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.headline: No human or animal data were collected, so ethical approval was not sought.

sections.body: Thanapong Intharah contributed to conceptualization, methodology, software, validation, formal analysis, investigation, data curation, visualization, original and review writing, project administration and funding acquisition. Zhichao Gao contributed to conceptualization and methodology. Yiliang Liu contributed to conceptualization and validation. Hao Dong provided supervision. The statement lists each author's contributions using the CRediT categories.
sections.heading: CRediT authorship contribution statement
sections.headline: Intharah led most roles, Gao and Liu contributed to conceptualization, and Dong supervised the work.

sections.body: T. Intharah, Z. Gao and H. Dong developed SonoSPADE. The study uses it with its method unchanged, as the texture stage of its standard simulation engine. The authors declare no other known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The disclosure matters because comparisons against SonoSPADE are not independent of its authors, as the discussion also notes.
sections.heading: Declaration of competing interest
sections.headline: Three authors developed SonoSPADE, which this study uses unchanged as its texture stage.

sections.body: The authors used Claude Code to draft and edit the text, write and test the testbed and analysis code, and run the experiments and analyses. The tool ran Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 5.5, as the commit history records. It also checked references against Crossref and PubMed. The authors reviewed the text in successive drafts, checked the code through its test suite on Linux, Windows and macOS, and ran scripts that rebuild every table and figure data file. The authors take full responsibility for the published content.

sections.headline: Claude Code helped draft text, write and test code, and run analyses, and the authors reviewed all content.

sections.body: The appendix gives the 13 training cases and six held-out cases, and renders of the four reference texture stages. It details the controls: independent target speckle, a second gap-cause family, a second imaging plane, tissue-anchored and shared speckle, the hill-climb, the base fit, and keep-best error. Its tables compare keep-best error with final error at 12 and 36 steps, and list the lowest-error pipelines. All control results are exploratory. The supplement gives the testbed details and the designs of these evaluations.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists the case split, control details, gap-cause and imaging-plane tests, and keep-best error tables.
